RagShortTexts: In 1264 Mudejar Muslims revolted across Andalusia and Murcia, secretly backed by Granada.

Variants.Content: In 1264 Alfonso X of Castile pressed ahead with forced deportations of Mudejar communities in Andalusia and Murcia, and the response was a rising across both regions. The rebels coordinated their attacks and drew secret support from Muhammad I of Granada, while Marinid volunteers crossed the Strait to fight. Christian garrisons were caught unprepared. At Jerez the Castilian garrison was massacred, and Murcia slipped out of royal control. The revolt exposed how fragile Castilian authority remained among the Mudejar population of the south.

Alfonso X could not hold the uprisings alone, so he appealed to James I of Aragon, whose seasoned forces were sent to subdue Murcia. The rebellion ended the tolerance that had marked Castile's dealings with its Muslim subjects, and the expulsion of Muslims from southern lands followed. Lords who had profited from Mudejar labour had to find new arrangements for their estates.

The rising was savage from the first night. Men died to daggers in the town garrisons, and the counterattacks were just as merciless, with cavalry sweeping through rebel villages. Nobody gave quarter on either side. On a night watch in such a town, keep your back to a wall and trust no one who comes to the gate unannounced.

Thousands of Mudéjar peasant families fled along mountain trails toward the safety of Granada with whatever they could carry on donkey-back. Century-old irrigated fields fell barren as northern Christian settlers arrived.
